tactics.claim: Fix conversion rate before spending on traffic, because raising 1% to 3% cuts cost per acquisition by two-thirds and makes every other marketing channel affordable.
tactics.mechanism: Traffic costs money or time per visitor; conversion rate is a multiplier applied to all of it, so improving the multiplier improves the economics of every channel simultaneously and retroactively.
tactics.evidence: Worked arithmetic (£1/click, 1% vs 3% conversion, £100 vs £33 cost per lead) plus a claim that Exposure Ninja regularly builds sites converting at 2–10% versus a common 0.5%. No named cases.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, so age is irrelevant — but this exactly restates the operating reality already governing the business: paid spend is gated behind Tracking → CRO → Offer/AOV → Traffic. Promoting it into a skill adds no new mechanism or artifact and would duplicate a rule that is already the default. The lead-gen framing (cost per lead, form fills) also does not match a 12-SKU ecommerce catalogue.

tactics.rejectReason: Restates the already-adopted gating rule (CRO before traffic) with no new mechanism or artifact; lead-gen cost-per-lead framing does not map to a 12-SKU consumables catalogue.

tactics.claim: Score every conversion page against a fixed six-item rubric — credibility, lure (what do I get and is it attractive at this price), objection handling, social proof, ease of use / application instructions, and result (is it clear what they get when they act) — and fix whichever items are missing or weak.
tactics.mechanism: Conversion failure is usually a missing element rather than bad design; each item corresponds to a separate reason a visitor stalls, so walking a named list forces you to identify the actual leak instead of polishing whichever element you happen to notice.
tactics.evidence: Presented as the course's 'qualified customer closer' roadmap, then applied live to three lead-gen pages and to a real screen-protector product page and homepage, item by item — including the observation that a £60/mo LeadPages page beat a £20,000 site on five of six elements, and two concrete failures found (shipping/currency inconsistency, undemonstrated result). Practitioner-derived rubric, no test data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class — a diagnostic rubric, age irrelevant. Free, solo-executable, needs no traffic or attribution, and applies to the Shopify PDP, collection pages, and the Amazon listing/A+ block where two-thirds of revenue sits. Held at 7 because marketing-conversion-friction-audit already owns roughly half the items (risk, proof, returns visibility, the four-term value equation); the additive value is the named checklist ordering plus the 'lure' and 'result' items — making explicit what happens after add-to-cart or after an email signup — so it belongs as an additional pass inside that skill rather than a new one, and at ~54 orders/month fixes are applied by judgement rather than tested.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add a six-item page scorecard (credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease/instructions, result) as a surface-level pass to run on the Shopify PDP, collection pages, and Amazon listing/A+ before making changes.

tactics.claim: If you do not give visitors an explicit reason to believe you are good, they cannot believe it — credibility must be manufactured on the page, not assumed.
tactics.mechanism: A stranger landing on your site has no information about you beyond what the page states, so absent stated proof they default to treating you as another interchangeable business.
tactics.evidence: Seminar anecdote where audience members asked how they know a business is good can only point to the logo. Assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, age irrelevant, and true — but it is the framing statement above the concrete devices rather than a testable action of its own.

tactics.rejectReason: Framing without an executable mechanism; every actionable form (before/after selection, meaningful specifics, credibility-marker placement, testimonial construction) is captured as a separate adopted tactic.

tactics.claim: Select or build proof whose 'before' state is one the target buyer recognises as their situation today and whose 'after' is the outcome they actually want — and remember the format can be a testimonial, case study or video, not only a photo pair.
tactics.mechanism: Identification is what makes proof persuasive: a viewer who sees themselves in the before state accepts the after state as available to them, whereas a before state that does not match their situation reads as evidence about someone else. A single quote that names the prospect's current state does both the resonance and the proof job that generic praise cannot.
tactics.evidence: Bill Phillips fitness camp before/after pages, plus the AV company example where an events director's testimonial ('the best AV company I've ever dealt with') functions as an implicit before/after for another events director. Practitioner analysis, no conversion data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable persuasion principle, age irrelevant, and free to apply on Shopify PDP imagery/copy and Amazon secondary image and A+ slots — the surfaces carrying ~$1,800/mo of Amazon revenue. It works on dozens of reviews rather than thousands: RSC's reviews naturally contain the before ('every natural deodorant I tried quit by noon') and the after ('made it through a 12-hour shift'). The non-photo permission matters because honest photographic before/afters are hard to produce solo for body care. Not higher because the existing review-mining and product-image-stack skills already own extraction and the transformation format — this only supplies the selection rule.

targetSkill.name: marketing-review-mining
targetSkill.description: Add a selection rule: pick proof (review quote, photo pair, or video) where the 'before' is the buyer's recognisable current situation and the 'after' is the outcome they want, and note that testimonial text can carry the before/after structure when photography can't.

tactics.claim: Load proof with 'meaningful specifics' — exact figures (21% to 9% body fat, 30 lbs) plus seemingly irrelevant identifying detail such as age, occupation and location — because the irrelevant detail is what makes the claim feel real.
tactics.mechanism: Concrete, checkable-sounding detail signals a real person and a real event rather than a marketing construction; a specific figure is harder to dismiss than 'lost loads of fat', and biographical detail with no bearing on the result ('a fireman in California') signals an ordinary person rather than a paid guru.
tactics.evidence: Line-by-line teardown of a Bill Phillips testimonial explaining what each detail is doing, plus AV company testimonials that name both the company and the job title of the person quoted. Assertion with worked examples.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, zero cost, no traffic or attribution required — CRO-stage work. It extends the specificity rule already in marketing-conversion-copy-angles in a genuinely additive direction: that rule covers numbers in claim copy, this covers attribution detail on borrowed proof. Directly executable by pulling existing Shopify and Amazon reviews and displaying them with the reviewer's stated context ('switched off aluminium three years ago', 'works through 12-hour shifts') rather than a bare anonymous star quote. Not higher because the number half overlaps the existing rule and RSC can only display detail reviewers actually volunteered — inventing it is dishonest and an Amazon policy risk.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-copy-angles
targetSkill.description: Extend the specificity rule to borrowed proof: display reviewer context (occupation, tenure, situation) alongside the quote, using only detail the reviewer volunteered.

tactics.claim: Make the testimonial close the loop by explicitly crediting the product or mechanism for the result, rather than leaving the reader to infer the connection.
tactics.mechanism: A reader who sees an impressive outcome without a stated cause may attribute it to the person's effort, luck or something else entirely; naming the mechanism inside the quote transfers the credit to your product.
tactics.evidence: Notes that the fitness testimonial ends with 'Tim credits the simple yet effective 25-minute workouts, the balanced nutrition and the online peer support community' — described as deliberately making the causal link obvious. Assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, free, and it is a selection criterion rather than a writing licence — which is what makes it safe here. A solo operator can read RSC's whole review corpus in an afternoon and choose the quotes that name what actually worked ('the baking-soda-free one is the only thing that got me through the switch') over vaguer praise, then place them on the PDP, in Amazon A+ blocks and in post-purchase emails. Held at 6 because it is a filter applied to existing material rather than a new revenue mechanism, and fabricating or editing the causal sentence into a customer's quote is a real compliance risk in body care.

targetSkill.name: marketing-review-mining
targetSkill.description: Add a filter: prefer review quotes that explicitly credit the product or its mechanism for the result; select and honestly excerpt, never edit the causal sentence in.

tactics.claim: Spread your displayed proof across different ages, genders and situations, and include cases that pre-empt the specific belief that would disqualify a reader ('at age 50...' kills 'I'm too old for this').
tactics.mechanism: Every visitor silently asks whether the result applies to someone like them; a proof set covering multiple identities means each reader finds their own case, and a case that leads with the disqualifying attribute neutralises the objection before it forms.
tactics.evidence: Points out the fitness page alternates male and female subjects and opens one testimonial with 'at age 50'; explains what each choice defuses. Practitioner analysis, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, zero cost, and unusually well matched to the category's real disqualifiers — 'natural deodorant never works for someone who sweats as much as me', 'baking soda burns my skin', 'I gave up during the transition'. Those are exactly the beliefs blocking first purchase and reorder, and retention is the binding constraint. Executable today by curating existing Shopify and Amazon reviews into a proof set organised by objection rather than star rating, then placing them on the PDP and in the A+ block. Held at 7 because with a small corpus some objection slots will be empty — the gap becomes a prompt for the post-purchase review request, not something to fabricate.

targetSkill.name: marketing-review-mining
targetSkill.description: Add an organising rule: curate the displayed proof set by objection and buyer identity (heavy sweater, sensitive skin, transition quitter) rather than by star rating, and treat empty slots as review-request prompts.

tactics.claim: Inventory the credibility and social-proof assets you actually have (star rating and review count, awards, certifications, third-party testing, client or press logos, safe-checkout and payment badges, volume claims) and place at least one directly at every decision point — above the fold and immediately beside the button you expect people to click — instead of leaving them on an About or reviews page.
tactics.mechanism: Nobody wants to be the first person to take an action, and everywhere you ask for trust you must supply a reason to trust at the moment of the ask. Credibility markers are an instant shortcut requiring no reading, but a marker the visitor has to hunt for is never counted, and proof only removes the objection if it is physically present when the objection fires.
tactics.evidence: Client example where NHS, Deloitte, Lafarge and BBC logos were buried on an About page and moved into the hero and headline copy; Exposure Ninja's own awards and Google review display beside CTAs; National Accident Helpline teardown (Trustpilot in the hero, trust score and reviews in the sidebar beside the form, testimonials underneath); an ecommerce PDP with an above-the-fold review widget, secure-checkout logos and a '500k sold' badge; and an email popup reading '42,000 other people get our tips'. Assertions and teardowns, no conversion figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (proof psychology and placement), age irrelevant. Purely editorial, zero cost, no traffic or attribution needed — CRO-stage work on the ~$875/mo Shopify PDP and the Amazon A+ block: move star rating and one verbatim quote adjacent to add-to-cart, add payment/secure-checkout badges above the fold, and put proof in the email capture popup. Held at 7 because RSC has no enterprise logos or press coverage and the volume-based variants ('500k sold', '42,000 subscribers') depend on scale it does not have — displaying a small review count or list size can undercut credibility, so the marker set must be chosen honestly (third-party testing, cruelty-free/made-in-USA certification, small-batch) rather than padded; Amazon also controls star placement on the larger channel.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add an inventory-then-place discipline: list every honest credibility marker the brand owns and put at least one above the fold and adjacent to each add-to-cart, subscribe toggle, and email-capture button; skip volume claims that scale can't support.

tactics.claim: The visual first impression of a site determines how visitors rate every other attribute of the business — product quality, customer service, staff, reviews, wait times — and you cannot judge your own site, so get an impartial outside opinion.
tactics.mechanism: With no other information available, visitors extrapolate from the only signal present; a polished design reads as evidence of investment and competence across the whole operation, and an amateur one reads as evidence of the opposite. Owners are too close to their own build to see which one they have.
tactics.evidence: Side-by-side of the same company's old and new site, where a room of people rated site B higher on every question asked — product, service, employee happiness, reviews, call queues — without knowing both were the same business. Anecdotal seminar demonstration; the rebuild cost ~£4,000 and the outcome is described in perception terms only, with no conversion data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (perception psychology), so age is not the limiter. The remedy the creator delivers — a £4,000 agency rebuild — is disqualified outright: no agency, no designer, no budget at ~$2,700/mo. What transfers is narrower but real and free: the halo argument says product photography and PDP presentation quality carry more weight than another copy tweak, and 'you cannot judge your own store' is actionable at zero cost by asking outsiders for a five-second first-impression read. Held to 5 because the headline execution is out of reach, the named tool (usertesting.com) is a paid dependency, and at ~54 orders/month any presentation change is unmeasurable.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add a halo/first-impression note: presentation quality colours perception of the product itself, so prioritise photography and PDP polish, and get free five-second outside impressions rather than trusting the owner's own eye.

tactics.claim: Remove conversion blockers — hard-to-find calls to action, unnecessary form fields, unclear next steps — to create a 'slippery slide' from landing to purchase.
tactics.mechanism: Every additional step, field or moment of hunting is a chance to abandon; stripping them lets an intent-carrying visitor slide through to conversion without friction.
tactics.evidence: Stated as the principle for a later video; no examples or data in this excerpt.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, but marketing-conversion-friction-audit already owns exactly this — express and guest checkout, decision fatigue from too many variants, information fatigue from over-long pages.

tactics.rejectReason: Preview-only restatement of coverage the existing friction-audit skill already holds; form-field reduction is a lead-gen concern for a store whose checkout is Shopify's.

tactics.claim: There is a second class of objection — objections to taking the conversion action itself, not to the product — so enumerate the visitor's top three fears about clicking your CTA and answer each one in the copy immediately around it.
tactics.mechanism: A visitor holds desire for the outcome on one side and fear, doubt and uncertainty on the other. Until the specific red flags (will this be low value, will someone pitch me, will I be embarrassed, what am I committing to) are answered, they will not act — and almost nobody will ask; they just leave and go somewhere they feel more assured. Web objections are driven by uncertainty about what happens next rather than by price.
tactics.evidence: Worked examples: a construction firm's 'request a free quote' with no service-area or next-step info; a claims firm's 'start my claim'; a kitchen firm's copy that explicitly makes the home survey optional; plus the creator's own three fears about their free website review (it'll be rubbish, it's nothing new, someone will pitch me) and the exact copy used to defuse each. Practitioner assertion, no conversion figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, age irrelevant. CRO-stage work requiring no spend, no traffic, no attribution. Distinct from the existing problem/solution inventory (problems with the product) and from the friction audit's returns/guarantee coverage: this is about fears attached to the specific act of clicking. Live surfaces are the Shopify add-to-cart, the email capture popup, and the subscribe-and-save toggle — 'will I get locked in', 'will you spam me', 'what if the scent is wrong', 'will the discount code fail'. Capped at 7 because Amazon (~$1,800/mo, the larger channel) controls its own buy box, so the gain is confined to the ~$875/mo Shopify side and the popup.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add an action-objection pass: list the top three fears attached to clicking each CTA (add-to-cart, subscribe toggle, popup) and answer them in the copy immediately surrounding that button.

tactics.claim: Make the conversion action the single most visible element above the fold — a bordered box with a high-contrast button and white space, placed where buyers already expect it (Amazon's top-right buy box) — never buried at the bottom of the page.
tactics.mechanism: Visitors are unfamiliar, busy and distracted, so they do not hunt; a buyer who has to scroll for the way to act mostly does not act. Amazon has already trained every shopper where the buy action lives, so matching that position makes comprehension instant and removes a step that offers the buyer nothing.
tactics.evidence: Three site walkthroughs with claimed rate bands (form buried at the bottom 0–1%, above-the-fold solicitor form 2–3%, strong lure above the fold 10–15%, one test site 33.7%), plus the Amazon product page cited as the convention-setter, a client 'get a quick quote' box, and the thought experiment of Amazon replacing its buy box with a phone number at the page bottom.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (layout convention and attention), not a fast-decaying platform mechanic — the Amazon buy-box convention has held for over a decade. Free and solo-executable: one theme pass to get add-to-cart, price, and the email-capture incentive above the fold and made the visual focal point on the Shopify PDP and homepage. Capped at 7 because the quoted UK lead-gen rate bands do not transfer to a $50.46-AOV consumable, at ~54 orders/month no placement change will be measurable, and it partly overlaps the existing rule about moving the guarantee above the fold next to add-to-cart — so treat it as one do-it-and-move-on layout pass.

targetSkill.name: marketing-page-cta-placement
targetSkill.description: New skill for conversion-action layout: make the primary ask the single most visible above-the-fold element in a conventional position, sized and contrasted so a distracted visitor cannot miss it.

tactics.claim: Word the call to action for the lowest perceived pain, not the highest perceived value — 'get a free quote' over 'book a free survey', 'try our 30-second claim checker' over 'start my claim' — and never ask for a step further down the buyer journey than the buyer currently needs.
tactics.mechanism: Every ask carries an implied cost: 'book a survey' implies a salesperson in your house, 'start my claim' implies deciding now with embarrassment or cost attached if you turn out to be wrong. A low-commitment verb reframes the click as investigation rather than decision, so the visitor can proceed without having settled anything — even though the underlying offer is identical.
tactics.evidence: ADT split test where 'get a free quote' beat 'book a free survey' by a claimed 60% uplift (audience had already established need and only wanted a price), plus a side-by-side of three claims-industry CTAs with 'try our 30-second claim checker' called 'perfect'. One split test, otherwise assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (persuasion / perceived risk), so the older test date doesn't matter. Directly actionable at zero cost on the email-capture button, the secondary PDP CTAs ('find your scent' as entry to a SKU-match quiz across 12 SKUs), and especially the subscription CTA where 'Subscribe' implies lock-in while 'Send a refill every 8 weeks — change or cancel anytime' does not. Since retention is the binding constraint and subscribe-and-save is the adopted retention lever, reducing implied commitment on that button is a real lever. Not higher because the primary ecommerce CTA is add-to-cart and cannot be softened, Amazon button copy is not editable, and at ~54 orders/month RSC cannot run the split test that produced the 60% figure.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add a CTA-wording rule: phrase every secondary ask for lowest implied commitment (investigation, not decision), especially the subscribe toggle and email capture button.

tactics.claim: When you have no testimonials, build credibility by describing the buyer's specific problem in extreme detail — hyper-niching on their situation earns trust the way a palm reader does, before any proof is shown.
tactics.mechanism: Accurately naming someone's situation signals that you have seen it many times before, which is the same inference a testimonial produces; the prospect concludes 'you understand me' and grants credibility without needing third-party evidence.
tactics.evidence: Worked example of an accountancy firm positioning for early-stage tech startups seeking investment, plus the palm-reader anecdote. Assertion, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable persuasion principle, age irrelevant, and it fills a genuine gap: existing copy skills cover calling the buyer out by name and attributing claims to an authority, but not the idea that problem articulation itself substitutes for proof — which matters for a brand with dozens rather than thousands of reviews. The natural-deodorant switch has an unusually detailed, nameable problem sequence (the two-week transition, the mid-afternoon check, residue on a dark shirt) already inventoried elsewhere; writing it out on the PDP and in Amazon bullets is free and needs no traffic.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-copy-angles
targetSkill.description: Add problem-articulation-as-proof: when review volume is thin, describe the buyer's exact situation in unusual detail so recognition substitutes for third-party evidence.

tactics.claim: Use your own background or origin story as a credibility and bonding asset — pick the elements of it your audience will recognise in themselves and put those in the marketing.
tactics.mechanism: Recognising a shared element of someone's story creates a felt closeness ('you're just like me') that functions like resonating with the buyer's before-state, so trust transfers without any external proof.
tactics.evidence: Personal anecdote: mentioning he was a professional drummer in seminars consistently drew musicians up to him afterwards; he infers a bonding effect. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, zero cost, and a solo operator is the one case where the founder story is genuinely available — it can go in the Amazon A+ Brand Story module, a PDP about-block, and the welcome email. The recognisable element is the one the buyer shares ('I switched off aluminium and every natural deodorant failed me, so I made this'). Held at 6 because it is unmeasurable at ~54 orders/month, it must not crowd out decision-relevant content per the information-fatigue rule, and it overlaps the existing authority-attribution entry mentioning founder formulation credentials.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-copy-angles
targetSkill.description: Add founder-story bonding: select the elements of the origin story the target buyer shares and place them in the A+ Brand Story module, a PDP block, and the welcome email — kept short so they don't displace decision-relevant content.

tactics.claim: Assume every subpage is an entry page for cold traffic — the credibility, social proof and offer that sit on the homepage must be repeated on the deep pages people actually land on, and proof belongs on the product or service pages rather than on a dedicated case-studies or reviews page nobody visits.
tactics.mechanism: Organic and paid visitors land directly on deep pages with zero brand context and nobody navigates down from the homepage, so any trust element living only on the homepage is invisible to the majority of buyers. Proof only works where the decision is made — and a buyer who never clicks through still absorbs credibility from seeing the logo or headline sitting next to the offer.
tactics.evidence: Live demonstration: a law firm's Trustpilot stars and award badges appear on the homepage but vanish on the commercial-contracts subpage that would actually rank in Google; plus screenshots of case studies embedded on a service page with client logos, and the assertion that case-study pages are among the least-visited on any site.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class and an unusually exact match: an Amazon listing and a Shopify PDP are both pure cold-traffic entry points with no homepage visit preceding them, and Amazon is the larger channel at ~$1,800/mo. Zero cost, solo-executable, no traffic or attribution required — it means the review quotes, third-party proof, transition-period guarantee and 'what this is' framing must each appear on every PDP and in the A+ content rather than once on the homepage or a policy page. It sharpens existing proof-placement work by naming which pages need the proof, which nothing currently owns.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add an entry-page rule: treat every PDP, collection page and Amazon listing as a cold-traffic landing page that must independently carry the proof, guarantee and category framing, rather than relying on the homepage or a policy page.

tactics.claim: Borrow credibility from a 'celebrity' who already has trust with your audience — an industry figure or publication, not a famous person — and present them in the context your audience already associates with them so they don't read as a salesperson.
tactics.mechanism: Trust already built with a familiar figure transfers to whatever they endorse, and keeping their native styling and setting preserves the illusion of a recommendation rather than an advertisement.
tactics.evidence: Alan Titchmarsh selling life insurance in a gilet holding a mug in a garden; explains the mug and garden as devices to avoid looking like a salesperson. Observational, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Requires a paid or negotiated partner and creative production a solo operator with no team, no designer and ~$2,700/mo revenue cannot fund.

tactics.rejectReason: Needs a paid spokesperson and production budget out of reach at ~$2,700/mo, and duplicates the authority-attribution entry already capped at 5 in marketing-conversion-copy-angles.

tactics.claim: Never make the ask a bare 'make an inquiry', 'email us' or 'subscribe to our newsletter' — offer a lure with real perceived value (buyer's guide, free postage, first-order discount, a free consultation you already do anyway) and append the tangible outcome to the ask ('request a free consultation and we'll show you how much you could save'); if you can't state how it moves the buyer toward their goal, it isn't compelling enough.
tactics.mechanism: A visitor has no reason to hand over contact details for a step that only advances the seller's journey. Perceived value comes from a visible, tangible next step, so naming the concrete thing they walk away with converts a procedural ask into an exchange the visitor wants to make.
tactics.evidence: Solicitor and construction-site examples with no lure and claimed 0–3% conversion versus PPI pages offering 'we find out if you had PPI' at claimed 10–15% and 33.7%; exhibition stand company already producing free 3D visuals but not advertising them; a law firm already running a free qualification chat it never mentions; plus rewritten CTA examples for funding, weight loss and IT cost saving.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle and true here, but marketing-offer-construction already carries 'never let the ask be a bare request-a-quote — give something in exchange for contact information', the three lead-magnet types, the 'describe it as a dream outcome in the buyer's own words' rule, and the 'give away something other people charge for' filter. The ecommerce examples given (buyer's guide, 10% off, free postage) are exactly what that skill already covers.

tactics.rejectReason: Fully duplicated by existing marketing-offer-construction coverage of lead-magnet selection and dream-outcome phrasing; re-adding it would degrade skill triggering.

tactics.claim: Choose the lure by whether the audience knows the scale of their problem — if they don't, offer something that diagnoses it (audit, mockup, visual); if they do, offer a road map or plan to reach the goal.
tactics.mechanism: The offer has to be the next station on the buyer's own journey; a diagnostic serves someone who cannot yet see the size of the problem, while someone who already knows needs a route to the outcome.
tactics.evidence: Own marketing-review offer, exhibition-stand client's free 3D mockup, and a funding client's 'free consultation plus a funding plan'; anecdotal.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle but the selection rule is already covered twice: marketing-awareness-level-messaging owns diagnosing problem-aware versus solution-aware readers, and marketing-offer-construction's three lead-magnet types are the same menu. The concrete artifacts named are service deliverables with no low-cost equivalent for a 12-SKU consumable beyond the scent-match quiz already listed.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicates awareness-level diagnosis and the existing lead-magnet type menu; named artifacts are service-business deliverables.

tactics.claim: Spell out on the page exactly what happens after the visitor acts — who contacts them, how, when, through which channel, and what they can change or cancel — because if you don't tell people what they will get, they fill the gap with their worst fear.
tactics.mechanism: Unknown process is priced as worst-case process. Stating the sequence explicitly answers several unvoiced objections at once — I don't have time, I don't want someone at my house, I don't want to be cornered — without the visitor ever having to raise them.
tactics.evidence: Specific recommended wording the creator says 'we found increases your conversion rate' ('fill in the details below and one of the team will be in touch to arrange a time convenient to you, by phone, Skype or in person'), plus the kitchen-design and free-site-survey examples where making the home visit explicitly optional removes the fear. No figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class. Its native form is lead-gen forms, which RSC does not run, but it transfers cleanly to the two live Shopify surfaces: the email capture popup (what arrives, how often, from whom) and the subscribe-and-save option (when it ships, when you are billed, how to skip or cancel, stated at the point of choice rather than in a policy page). Zero cost, solo-executable, CRO/Offer stage. Not higher because it partially overlaps the existing rule about stating returns and cancellation terms plainly — the additive part is stating the sequence of what happens next, not just the exit terms.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add a what-happens-next rule: state the post-click sequence (what arrives, when, from whom, how to change or cancel) at the point of the ask for the popup and subscribe-and-save toggle.

tactics.claim: When offering a discount for an email signup, defuse the spam objection by naming what you will actually send and how often ('occasional tips on how to do X') instead of leaving the newsletter undescribed.
tactics.mechanism: The visitor's default assumption about an undescribed newsletter is 'the same pitch twice a day forever', which is a negative value being weighed against the 10% discount. Describing the content as something that moves them toward their goal replaces the assumed cost with a stated benefit, raising opt-in rate without deepening the discount.
tactics.evidence: Stated directly as the ecommerce application of the objection-handling framework, with example wording. Assertion only, no opt-in rate data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class. The Shopify email capture popup is a live, zero-cost surface, and list growth feeds the retention constraint that binds here — repeat customers are 45–52% of revenue on an 18–22.5% repeat rate. Directly actionable: replace an undescribed '10% off' popup with a stated promise ('the two-week transition guide plus occasional restock reminders — no daily sales emails'). Held at 6 because the sibling rule about choosing a specific, desirable incentive already lives in offer-construction; the additive part is the objection-handling line beneath the incentive.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add a line under the email-capture incentive naming exactly what subscribers will receive and how often, to defuse the assumed-spam cost.

tactics.claim: In a multi-step form, ask about the visitor's problem first and only ask for personal contact details at step two, then show results at step three.
tactics.mechanism: Leading with name/email/phone reads as pure lead capture and gives nothing back, so people abandon. Leading with diagnostic questions makes the experience feel like a diagnosis the visitor is participating in; by the time details are requested they are already invested and the request has an obvious justification ('tell us where to send your result').
tactics.evidence: Walkthrough of a claims-site three-step form (injury details → your details → results), with the observation that the 'results' step is really a promise of a follow-up call, which also pre-authorises that call. Single example, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (form sequencing psychology), age irrelevant and free. It has exactly one real application here: the scent/SKU-match quiz already named as a candidate lead magnet across the 12-SKU catalog — ask the two or three fit questions first (current deodorant, sensitivity, scent preference), request the email at the end, deliver the recommendation. Scored 5 because RSC runs no multi-step form today, so this is conditional on building the quiz, and at ~54 orders/month the completion-rate effect can never be measured.

targetSkill.name: marketing-lead-capture-forms
targetSkill.description: New skill for lead-capture form design; include the sequencing rule — diagnostic questions first, contact details second, result third — applied to the scent/SKU-match quiz.

tactics.claim: Reframe and advertise the valuable steps you already perform but never mention — you don't need to add anything to your process, just position what already exists as a stated benefit.
tactics.mechanism: Value the buyer cannot perceive earns nothing. An unadvertised deliverable costs the same whether or not it is stated, so stating it is pure free lift in perceived value.
tactics.evidence: Exhibition stand company anecdote — they were already producing free 3D visuals and simply weren't putting it on the website; plus reframing an existing 30-minute qualification call as 'the free consultation'.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle and true, but already covered twice in existing skills with better source material: the London Underground entry in marketing-conversion-friction-audit and the buried-lifetime-warranty entry in marketing-offer-construction.

tactics.rejectReason: Near-duplicate of existing entries in conversion-friction-audit and offer-construction; re-adding would degrade triggering accuracy.

tactics.claim: Run the customer-mindset exercise — put yourself in a specific buying scenario and list every question you would need answered before contacting the first supplier you find.
tactics.mechanism: Sellers assume people with questions will get in touch and ask. In reality only a small minority will; most do quick scouting and leave if they can't establish you're in the right ballpark. Simulating the scenario in detail surfaces the questions that must be pre-answered on the page.
tactics.evidence: The broken-boiler-with-a-newborn thought experiment, run live, producing a list of objections (cost, speed, qualification, service area, boiler type). Teaching exercise, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle but marketing-problem-solution-inventory already owns exactly this generative move — walking the buyer's before/during/after sequence in detail to enumerate every problem and quit-reason — with a richer generator plus the commit-to-answering-every-obstacle rule.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of the existing problem/solution enumeration exercise; a second near-identical generator would compete for triggering.

tactics.claim: On the page where you are asking for the conversion, don't sell your company — the page's only job is to get them to take the one action.
tactics.mechanism: Credentials and company pitch compete for attention with the single action you want, splitting the focal point.
tactics.evidence: Observation about the 30-second claim checker page: 'they're not selling you their solicitors firm, all they're doing is getting you to do the test.' Assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, but marketing-product-image-stack already states the one-goal-one-persona rule, marketing-email-design-production carries 'exactly one offer or ask per email', and marketing-conversion-friction-audit carries the information-fatigue rule about ordering page content by decision-relevance.

tactics.rejectReason: Would triple-cover the single-focus rule already present in three existing skills, with no new mechanism.

tactics.claim: Collect and display proof about the specific thing you are asking people to claim — the free review, the consultation, the bundle — rather than generic praise for the business, and where volume allows, an aggregate rating of that free thing.
tactics.mechanism: Proof only removes the objection it actually addresses. A review of the brand answers 'are they legitimate'; a review of the offer answers 'is claiming this thing worth my time', which is the question the visitor is actually stalling on at the CTA. Knowing the free thing will be rated also forces you to raise its quality.
tactics.evidence: Exposure Ninja's own review-request page, where every testimonial is about the free review service rather than the agency; the counselling example ('what would you say to other people thinking of getting a free consultation?'); plus their practice of asking for a review at the end of the free review email and a generic NPS-on-your-newsletter suggestion (Delighted). Assertion, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class. Concretely usable and free: pull quotes specifically about the starter bundle, the refill cadence, or surviving the transition period and place them beside that exact offer rather than reusing one brand-level five-star quote everywhere. Ties into the existing review-mining workflow. Held at 6 because with ~54 orders/month there may be very few offer-specific quotes yet, solicitation is restricted on Amazon, and the aggregate-NPS variant is not viable — a score drawn from a handful of responses is not credible proof and adds a survey tool against ~$2,700/mo revenue.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add offer-specific proof: display quotes about the exact thing being requested (bundle, subscription, transition guide) next to that ask, not generic brand praise; skip aggregate scores until sample size supports them.

tactics.claim: Build review volume over time, because buyers pick the option with more reviews even when its average rating is lower.
tactics.mechanism: Volume of reviews is read as volume of prior buyers, and social safety comes from crowd size rather than from rating quality.
tactics.evidence: The two-books-on-Amazon seminar demonstration — audiences unanimously pick the book with more reviews and a worse average. Anecdotal.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, but the actionable instruction ('email customers links to your review pages') is already owned by the review-collection tactic in marketing-conversion-friction-audit, and the comparative claim depends on scale that does not exist here — RSC will not out-review Native or Dr. Squatch on Amazon.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicates the existing review-collection entry and depends on review scale RSC cannot reach against category incumbents.

tactics.claim: Do not innovate on layout or navigation — give visitors exactly what they expect where they expect it, because anything they have never seen before is by definition not easy to use.
tactics.mechanism: Familiarity is the whole of ease of use. Novel patterns force the visitor to learn your interface before they can convert, which they will not do; award-winning originality and conversion rate are unrelated metrics.
tactics.evidence: Anecdote about a law firm's expensive, award-winning French-agency site whose non-obvious hamburger menu produced a massive bounce rate; contrasted with a conventional site the agency built that converted at 9.2% in month one versus 2.48% for its predecessor. Anecdotal, single case, unaudited figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, age irrelevant. Directly useful for a solo operator choosing or editing a Shopify theme with no designer: it is a rule that says spend nothing on custom design and keep the standard PDP pattern. Zero cost, no traffic requirement, CRO stage. Not higher because it is a constraint on what not to do rather than a change that itself produces revenue.

targetSkill.name: marketing-page-cta-placement
targetSkill.description: Include a convention rule: keep standard Shopify PDP and navigation patterns, avoid custom or novel layouts, since familiarity is what makes a page easy to use.

tactics.claim: Repeat the same single call to action many times down the page — header button, hero, mid-page banner buttons, sticky bar at the bottom — so a distracted visitor cannot miss it.
tactics.mechanism: Readers decide at different scroll depths and are too distracted to scroll back; multiple instances of the identical action catch each of them at the moment of intent without splitting attention, because every instance points at one destination.
tactics.evidence: Walkthrough of a site with a CTA box, header button, two banner buttons, phone number, live-call widget and sticky bottom banner, credited with 9.2% conversion in month one versus 2.48% for the site it replaced. Single client case, no isolation of this variable.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class. Executable free on Shopify (sticky add-to-cart, a repeated ATC below the ingredient and timeline blocks) and consistent with the one-ask-per-asset rule already adopted, since every instance is the same ask. Needs reconciling with the information-fatigue rule: repeat the button, not the content. Capped at 7 because the 2.48%-to-9.2% figure comes from a service lead-gen site and does not transfer to a consumable PDP, and at ~54 orders/month the change cannot be measured.

targetSkill.name: marketing-page-cta-placement
targetSkill.description: Include CTA repetition: place the same single ask at multiple scroll depths (hero, mid-page, sticky) so intent is captured wherever the reader decides — repeat the button, not the content.

tactics.claim: Form length is a dial in both directions: conversion falls steadily from three to ten fields, but one or two fields also converts worse because a bare name-and-email form signals 'you are about to be pitched' rather than 'you will receive a diagnosis' — and where fulfilment is costly, extra fields are a deliberate filter against unserious requests.
tactics.mechanism: Each field is effort, so more fields suppress volume; but perceived value comes from the offer feeling like a personalised assessment, which requires asking about their situation. Asking only for contact details reveals that contact is all you want. Because the extra effort is only spent by serious people, the same fields double as a qualification gate.
tactics.evidence: A HubSpot study chart of conversion rate by field count showing the 1-2 field dip and the 3-10 decline, plus Exposure Ninja's own decision to keep a long form on its free review because each review costs real time and money. Third-party study of unstated age, plus practitioner reasoning.

rscFit.reasoning: The underlying logic (perceived value of a diagnosis, effort as a filter) is durable-principle class, but the specific HubSpot curve is old lead-generation data that does not transfer to a $50.46-AOV consumable — hence 6 not 8. One real application: the scent/SKU-match quiz and any free-sample request contemplated as email-capture incentives, where a few questions make the output feel like a recommendation and gate the COGS-bearing sample against tyre-kickers. Must never be applied to checkout, where the friction rules stand.

targetSkill.name: marketing-lead-capture-forms
targetSkill.description: Include the field-count dial: three to five situational questions outperform a bare email box for diagnostic offers and filter out unserious requests for COGS-bearing samples; never apply to checkout.

tactics.claim: Ask only for information you will actually use — no phone field if nobody is going to call — and wherever possible use multiple choice or dropdowns instead of free-text areas, because conversion falls sharply with each text box.
tactics.mechanism: Unused fields suppress conversion for no return. Typing is far more effort than tapping a pre-written option, so replacing open text with selection preserves the information while cutting the cost of giving it.
tactics.evidence: HubSpot-style chart of conversion rate by number of text areas showing a steep decline; plus the reasoning that name is worth collecting because personalised emails get higher open and read rates. Study of unstated age plus assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, zero cost, solo-executable. Directly decides two live things: the Shopify popup collects email plus first name (name is used, because the post-purchase and win-back emails carrying the 18–22.5% repeat rate personalise better) and nothing else, and any quiz is all tap-to-choose. The 'no phone number without a team to call' rule is exactly right for a solo operator. Not higher because it is a one-time settings-level change whose effect at ~54 orders/month will never be readable.

targetSkill.name: marketing-lead-capture-forms
targetSkill.description: Include the field-selection rule: collect only fields that are actually used downstream, and prefer tap-to-choose options over free text.

tactics.claim: Sell a free offer as hard as a paid one — a whole page of what's included, what results to expect, and testimonials, because 'free' does not make people want it.
tactics.mechanism: Cost is only one objection. A free thing still demands time, attention and contact details, so the visitor still needs to be convinced the outcome is worth those, which requires explicit description of what they get plus proof that others found it worthwhile.
tactics.evidence: Walkthrough of the Exposure Ninja free-review page showing description, expected results and a stack of offer-specific testimonials, with the remark that 'just because it's free doesn't mean it's easy to get people to sign up for it.' Assertion plus own-asset teardown.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, and directly corrective for a lead-magnet strategy already adopted: the transition-period guide, sample, and scent-match quiz each need real copy and proof rather than a one-line popup. Zero cost, no traffic or attribution needed. Held at 6 because marketing-offer-construction already covers choosing and naming the incentive — the additive claim is only that the incentive needs its own selling copy and proof.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add: give every free offer its own selling copy — what's included, what result to expect, and proof — rather than assuming 'free' is persuasion enough.

tactics.claim: Build a repeatable multi-step sales process that turns a lead into a buyer — assessment call, check-in, written proposal, closing check-in — collapsing the first two steps when the lead already knows they need what you sell.
tactics.mechanism: A structured sequence of increasingly valuable interactions builds trust and momentum and surfaces objections before the proposal lands, so the sale becomes the natural end of the process rather than a separate persuasion event.
tactics.evidence: Exposure Ninja's own eight-year-refined process plus three client examples (exhibition stands, bespoke travel, PPI claims). The creator explicitly states this is 'relevant only for service companies'.

rscFit.reasoning: Assumes a human sales pipeline with consultations, proposals and a team to deliver them. RSC is a solo operator selling a $50.46-AOV consumable with no assessment, proposal or closing call anywhere in the purchase path; the creator himself scopes this to service companies.

tactics.rejectReason: Requires a service-business sales pipeline and staff that don't exist; the ecommerce equivalent (sequenced second asks) is already owned by marketing-upsell-offer-design.

tactics.claim: Assume every visitor is distracted and unfamiliar ('Homer Simpson'), and watch user-testing videos of real people using your site to see how confused they actually are.
tactics.mechanism: Owners find their own site intuitive because they built it; watching strangers narrate their confusion reveals that clarity, not sophistication of audience, determines conversion.
tactics.evidence: Anecdotes about watching user-testing recordings and about clients insisting their scientist or sophisticated audiences don't need obvious CTAs. Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: The actionable conclusion — make the CTA obvious and conventional — is already captured by the layout tactics adopted here. What remains is motivational framing or a research method needing testing tooling and a visitor pool RSC does not have at ~54 orders/month.

tactics.rejectReason: Actionable half duplicates the adopted CTA-placement and conventional-layout tactics; the research method requires paid tooling and traffic volume RSC lacks.

tactics.claim: Choose the delivery format for what a new lead receives — phone/Zoom call, in-person meeting, emailed presentation, or a free product trial — based on scalability and perceived risk; start with a live call while you're still learning what the asset needs to contain.
tactics.mechanism: Live formats give real-time feedback so you can calibrate depth and content; emailed assets are lowest perceived risk because the recipient does no work and can decline by not replying.
tactics.evidence: Their own history — website and marketing reviews first delivered by phone to learn the right level, then productised into an emailed video review. Anecdote, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, but channel and business-model mismatch: RSC sells a $50.46 physical consumable with no consultation, proposal or sales call behind any form. The one transferable fragment (low-friction asks convert better) is already owned by offer-construction and the friction audit.

tactics.rejectReason: Presumes a service lead-fulfilment asset and sales conversation that don't exist for a transactional consumables brand.

tactics.claim: If you offer a free trial of a product that requires setup, engineer the onboarding to be painless, step-by-step and almost game-like so users feel a sense of completion.
tactics.mechanism: The user's perception of how much work stands between them and the result — not product quality — is what kills trial conversion; visible incremental completion keeps them moving.
tactics.evidence: CRM comparison anecdote: Zoho's free trial put them off, Infusionsoft's paid setup fee got them committed. Personal preference, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: The general point (compress perceived effort to first result) is durable but is already the explicit core of marketing-post-purchase-onboarding and the time/effort terms in the friction audit. A deodorant has no setup task to gamify.

tactics.rejectReason: No setup task exists for a consumable; the transferable mechanism is already owned by marketing-post-purchase-onboarding.

tactics.claim: Ask what a new lead is most scared of the moment they convert, then open the thing you send them by doing the exact opposite — 'this is not a pitch', or an email that says 'we don't want to spam you, click here to choose how often you hear from us'.
tactics.mechanism: Becoming a lead does not remove fear; the two dominant fears are being pitched and being spammed. Naming the fear and immediately handing back control removes the objection before it forms, so the recipient reads the rest of the asset with their guard down instead of scanning for the sales trap.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus worked examples (claims company opener, email frequency chooser). No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, age irrelevant. Usable on two live zero-cost surfaces: the Shopify email-capture popup and the welcome email, where a frequency-choice link is a real solo-implementable Klaviyo preference page that protects a small list from unsubscribes — and list health feeds the binding retention constraint. Capped at 6 because marketing-conversion-copy-angles already covers negative framing; the additive move is the immediate reversal plus the preference-choice artifact, neither measurable at ~54 orders/month.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add: open the first delivered asset (welcome email) by naming the recipient's dominant fear and reversing it — no-pitch statement plus a frequency-preference link.

tactics.claim: Seed the fact that you sell the paid solution throughout any free asset you give away — state it in the opening, thread proof and case studies through the middle, and state the explicit next step at the end.
tactics.mechanism: Educational content that never mentions you sell the solution leaves recipients genuinely unaware they can buy; seeding early sets context, mid-asset proof builds the case while the reader is engaged, and the closing next step converts built-up intent instead of leaving it stranded.
tactics.evidence: Their own iteration history — recipients of the free review asked 'do you actually do this for people?', which forced the seeding change; described as tested through 'various iterations' and now 'the best option without a doubt'. No numbers.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class. Directly applicable to the free educational assets RSC can produce at zero cost — a transition-period guide as the popup incentive, the post-purchase education email, an Amazon A+ education block — exactly the assets a solo operator writes as pure education and then forgets to attach a purchase path to. Held at 6 because email-design-production already mandates multiple CTAs per email and offer-construction owns lead-magnet selection; the additive part is the placement pattern applied to educational content.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add a seeding pattern for free educational assets: state what you sell in the opening, thread proof through the middle, and close with the explicit purchase next step.

tactics.claim: Script every sales call your team makes — at minimum a fixed list of questions that must be answered — and run the process yourself first to find what works before handing it to staff.
tactics.mechanism: Unstructured calls produce inconsistent results; a minimum question set gives structure without robotic delivery, and founder-run testing produces the script that gets handed over.
tactics.evidence: Assertion from running their own sales team; no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Explicitly requires a sales team. RSC is a solo operator with no team and no phone sales channel at all.

tactics.rejectReason: Hard reject: requires a sales team and a phone sales channel that do not exist.

tactics.claim: A near-100% sales conversion rate on leads is a red flag, not a win — it means your marketing funnel is too narrow; widening the funnel should be expected to lower conversion rate while raising total sales.
tactics.mechanism: Only highly self-qualified prospects reach a narrow funnel, and very few people have the tenacity to self-qualify; a wider lure brings in more unqualified people but also more qualified ones, so absolute sales rise even as the percentage falls.
tactics.evidence: IT support company client anecdote — more leads, lower sales conversion rate, treated as the expected and correct outcome. Anecdote, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable diagnostic principle, but it is a top-of-funnel widening argument aimed at lead-gen businesses, and RSC's gated sequence puts Traffic last behind Tracking, CRO and Offer/AOV. Retention, not funnel width, is the binding constraint, and with attribution not yet working there is no way to act on the diagnosis.

tactics.rejectReason: Top-of-funnel diagnostic gated behind Traffic, which RSC has not reached; unusable without working attribution.

tactics.claim: Build a Plan B for monetising the unqualified leads a wider funnel produces: create a cheaper product such as a training course, refer them to competitors for commission, or drop them into a long nurture sequence.
tactics.mechanism: Unqualified leads are a fixed cost of a wide funnel, so a secondary monetisation path recovers revenue from people you cannot serve directly.
tactics.evidence: Their own Marketing You training site plus reciprocal agency referral commissions. Anecdote, no revenue figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Each branch fails a stated constraint: building a new product contradicts the adopted 'don't add products, add ways to offer what you have' gate; referring buyers to competing deodorant brands is nonsensical for a $2,700/mo CPG; and the nurture branch duplicates the email and retention skills.

tactics.rejectReason: Every branch violates an existing constraint (no new products, no competitor referrals) or duplicates adopted email/retention coverage.

tactics.claim: Run a long-horizon 'indoctrination' email sequence indefinitely — weekly for years if necessary — because a meaningful share of leads convert only after a very long delay.
tactics.mechanism: Not everyone is ready now; consistent presence over months and years keeps you in their world until circumstances change, at which point you are the logical choice.
tactics.evidence: Claims people have been on their list six years before becoming clients, and their largest client returned five years after a free review. Anecdotes, no cohort data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, but calibrated to a £10k/month agency retainer where one five-year conversion pays for the whole list. At a $50.46 AOV with a small list and a consumable reordered in weeks, the relevant nurture horizon is months — already owned by the seasonal re-wrapper tactic and the win-back tactic in retention-offers.

tactics.rejectReason: Economics assume a high-ticket service; the months-horizon version for a consumable is already covered by existing scarcity/retention skills.

tactics.claim: Install dedicated call-tracking software with dynamic number insertion (ResponseTap, ~£250/mo) so every inbound phone call is attributed to entry page, converting page, source, keyword and campaign and pushed into Analytics as a conversion, with call recording for QA — or approximate it free by tracking clicks on the phone-number link or using a Google forwarding number.
tactics.mechanism: Phone calls are otherwise untrackable — a visitor typing your number into their handset breaks the session link — so swapping in a per-session virtual number is the only way to tie a call back to the traffic that produced it; click-tracking and forwarding numbers give a rough count without per-session attribution.
tactics.evidence: Feature walkthrough plus the claim it is the most powerful option they have found across many clients, with explicit ~£250/mo price and the caveat it only pays off at meaningful lead volume and PPC spend. The free alternatives are asserted as less 'scientific'.

rscFit.reasoning: RSC takes no sales calls and sells transactionally on Shopify and Amazon — there is no phone conversion to attribute. The tool costs ~£250/mo against ~$2,700/mo total revenue and its whole value is Google Ads keyword attribution, which sits behind the Traffic gate that has not been reached; the free approximations also presume a running Ads account. Platform-mechanics class with 2020-era pricing and integrations.

tactics.rejectReason: No phone conversion path exists; recurring cost is disproportionate to revenue and the value depends on paid search spend that is gated.

tactics.claim: Add a triggered callback widget (LiveCall) that lets a visitor enter their number and be called back within seconds, which lifts both widget calls and direct phone calls.
tactics.mechanism: Removing the effort of dialling at the moment of intent captures leads who would not call; the widget's visible presence also signals that calling is welcome.
tactics.evidence: Practitioner claim of observing a lift in direct phone calls as well as widget calls across client sites; pricing quoted at $49–59/mo. No figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Explicitly requires 'people on the phones ready to go right now' — a solo operator with no team cannot man it, and there is no phone-sale motion for a $50.46 AOV deodorant order. Also a paid monthly tool against ~$2,700/mo revenue.

tactics.rejectReason: Requires staffed phone coverage and a phone sales motion that don't exist, plus a recurring cost against tiny revenue.

tactics.claim: Install free live chat (Tawk.to), restrict it to set opening hours so it takes messages when you're offline, and use the mobile app so you're not tied to a desk.
tactics.mechanism: Live chat answers objections at the moment they arise; scheduling and message capture stop it from becoming an always-on obligation.
tactics.evidence: Assertion that the free tool is as capable as paid alternatives. No conversion data.

rscFit.reasoning: Free and technically solo-installable, but at ~54 orders/month Shopify chat sessions will be sparse and the lift unmeasurable, while every session interrupts a solo operator. Amazon (~$1,800/mo) has no chat surface. The objections it would answer — transition period, staining, scent choice — are better answered permanently in PDP FAQ copy and post-purchase email.

tactics.rejectReason: Traffic volume too low to justify the interrupt cost; the same objections are better handled permanently in PDP copy already covered elsewhere.

tactics.claim: Put a sticky sitewide alert bar at the top or bottom of every page carrying one unmissable call to action or offer, because a bar converts worse than an in-page form but far better than having nothing.
tactics.mechanism: A persistent bar is present on every page and every device regardless of where the visitor entered or how far they scroll, so the primary ask can never be missed; it also requires no template surgery to deploy.
tactics.evidence: Live example on a client site showing a bottom bar with call/email/callback options plus a reviews widget; explicit admission that an in-page form converts better, framed as 'worth testing'. No numbers.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (offer placement), and the implementation is free — Shopify themes ship an announcement bar, so the 2020-era tool reference doesn't matter. Useful for making the current bundle, the free-shipping threshold, or the transition-period guarantee visible on every page rather than buried on the PDP — CRO/Offer-stage work with no spend. Capped at 6 because the lift is unmeasurable at ~54 orders/month, it only touches the ~$875/mo Shopify side, and a bar carrying a permanent discount would fight the warning against training the list to wait for markdowns.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add: use the Shopify announcement bar to carry one sitewide ask or offer (free-shipping threshold, guarantee, current bundle) on every page — never a permanent discount.

tactics.claim: Never write a page title, heading, or nav label that assumes the visitor has context — name the full thing ('commercial contract solicitors', not 'commercial contracts', not 'commercial home').
tactics.mechanism: A cold visitor has no frame of reference, so a truncated or internal label leaves them asking 'commercial what?'. Spelling out the category and who it's for removes the comprehension gap before it costs you the visit, and it happens to match the phrases people actually search.
tactics.evidence: Two live examples on the same site ('commercial home' as a menu item, 'Commercial Contracts' as an H1) with the creator naming it 'a very common mistake'. Assertion, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, zero cost, and directly load-bearing on the surface producing most revenue: an Amazon title has to state the category and format outright ('aluminum-free natural deodorant, 2.65 oz stick'), and a Shopify PDP H1 or collection name like 'Fresh' tells a cold visitor nothing. Distinct from the specificity-and-numbers rule already in conversion-copy-angles, which is about quantifying a claim rather than naming the category for a reader with no context. Not higher because Amazon keyword conventions largely force this already, so the real gain is confined to Shopify PDP headings and collection labels.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-copy-angles
targetSkill.description: Add a naming rule: every title, H1, collection name and nav label must state the full product category for a reader with zero context.

tactics.claim: A menu should help people choose, not act as a directory — cut the number of options and order them by what's most popular, never alphabetically.
tactics.mechanism: Past roughly six options a visitor can no longer hold the earlier ones in memory (the phone-menu problem), so long alphabetical lists force re-reading and stalling; ordering by demand puts the likely choice where it's seen first, and buyers often don't know the internal name for what they want.
tactics.evidence: Live walkthrough of a bloated alphabetical service menu where the most commercially important item ('tax') sits at the bottom purely because of its initial letter. Assertion plus the phone-menu analogy.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, free, solo-executable — Shopify menu and collection ordering can be set by best-sellers in minutes across 12 SKUs. Scored low because it is a narrow navigation-level restatement of the decision-fatigue rule already in conversion-friction-audit, the catalog is small enough that menu bloat is barely a problem, and Amazon controls navigation on the ~$1,800/mo channel.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Extend the decision-fatigue rule to navigation: keep menus short and order collections and variants by popularity, never alphabetically.

tactics.claim: Click the paid ads in your category and audit those landing pages, because advertisers are paying per click and are therefore forced to track and convert — their pages show you working conversion structure.
tactics.mechanism: Organic pages can survive being unconvertible; a page behind paid traffic cannot, so the elements persisting on advertisers' landing pages have been filtered by economic pressure rather than by taste.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated live: he searches 'commercial contracts lawyers', clicks the ads, and finds a cheap LeadPages page carrying Trustpilot proof, a stated volume claim ('helped 17,000 businesses'), testimonials, and an above-the-fold form — outscoring a £20,000 brand site.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class (competitive research practice), free and solo-executable. RSC already tracks Native, Dr. Squatch, Every Man Jack and Harry's in the ad library; this adds following their ads through to the landing page and auditing page structure, not just creative — feeding PDP layout and Amazon A+ decisions during the CRO stage with no spend. Scored 6 because it extends the existing ad-library gap analysis rather than being a new practice, and well-funded brands' paid pages include mechanics a solo operator cannot copy wholesale.

targetSkill.name: marketing-competitor-messaging-teardown
targetSkill.description: Add a step: follow competitor paid ads through to their landing pages and audit page structure (proof placement, offer, above-the-fold ask), not just the ad creative.

tactics.claim: Never make a mailto: email address the conversion action — use an on-page form, because clicking an email link opens whatever client is configured and produces no trackable data.
tactics.mechanism: A mailto link hands the conversion off to software you don't control, blocking visitors on the wrong client, and leaves no record of the lead or the page that produced it.
tactics.evidence: Live example: the firm's only CTA is an email address next to a named contact, so nobody can tell how the page performs. Assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle but the conversion action on a Shopify store is add-to-cart, not a contact form — there is no mailto-as-primary-CTA problem here, and Amazon forbids off-platform contact anyway. At best a housekeeping note on the contact page, which carries no revenue.

tactics.rejectReason: No mailto-as-primary-CTA exists on either channel; the fix carries no revenue for a transactional ecommerce store.

tactics.claim: Use a scheduling tool such as Calendly so prospects book straight into the sales team's diary, which improves show-up rates over a form that promises a callback.
tactics.mechanism: Locking the appointment into a calendar at the moment of intent removes the coordination step and the gap in which interest decays.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: There is no appointment, consultation or sales-call step in a $50.46 AOV consumables purchase, and no team to hold a diary.

tactics.rejectReason: Hard reject: no appointment step and no team exist in this business model.

tactics.claim: Conversion performance is unrelated to what you spent on the site — a £60/month landing page can out-convert a £20,000 custom build.
tactics.mechanism: Conversion is produced by the presence of specific elements (proof, lure, clarity, ease), which cost nothing to add and are orthogonal to design budget.
tactics.evidence: Side-by-side comparison of the expensive solicitors' site scoring poorly against a cheap LeadPages advertiser page scoring well on five of six elements.

rscFit.reasoning: Encouraging for a solo operator with no designer, and the underlying mechanism is already captured by the six-element scorecard adopted above. On its own it is framing rather than an action.

tactics.rejectReason: Framing with nothing to execute; the mechanism is already carried by the adopted six-element scorecard.

tactics.claim: Never assume established category demand means the product sells itself — do the full selling job on every product page, including commodity items like batteries.
tactics.mechanism: Visitors do not persuade themselves and have infinite alternatives with no obligation to convert; 'build it and they will come' fails online, so a page that only presents the product loses to one that argues for it.
tactics.evidence: Contrast between the Shark Proof page (novel product, heavily explained with benefit icons and scientific framing) and typical ecommerce stores selling known categories with thin copy. Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class and true for natural deodorant, but this is framing without a mechanism a solo operator can execute — it says 'try harder', not 'change X'. Everything actionable underneath it is already owned by marketing-awareness-level-messaging, marketing-conversion-copy-angles, marketing-problem-solution-inventory, and the benefit-icon format library in marketing-product-image-stack.

tactics.rejectReason: Exhortation without a distinct executable mechanism; all actionable substance already lives in existing awareness, copy-angle, objection and image-format skills.

tactics.claim: Give visitors who aren't ready to buy an alternative call to action that builds the email list, using a lure tied to a future purchase trigger — though skip it when the product is a cheap impulse buy.
tactics.mechanism: Most page visitors will never buy on this visit; capturing them against a future-need trigger means you own the audience at the moment the need actually appears.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus a hypothetical (tech-tips blog / new-iPhone alerts feeding screen-protector sales). Creator explicitly hedges that it may not be worth it for low-price impulse products.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, so age isn't the issue — the problem is duplication. marketing-offer-construction already covers choosing the email-capture incentive and the three lead-magnet types, which is the substantive part. The only novel element is the PDP placement of a secondary CTA, and the creator himself flags that low-price impulse categories may not warrant it.

tactics.rejectReason: Substantively duplicated by existing lead-magnet coverage in marketing-offer-construction; the creator hedges its applicability to low-price impulse products like this one.

tactics.claim: Handle the three standard ecommerce objections explicitly and adjacent to the buy button: return terms ('30 days easy returns'), dispatch speed ('same day dispatch'), and shipping cost ('free worldwide shipping').
tactics.mechanism: These are the objections nearly every ecommerce buyer holds silently; if they aren't answered where the decision is made, the buyer assumes the worst case on each and abandons rather than hunting for a policy page.
tactics.evidence: Live teardown naming each of the three on the example page and calling returns 'a massive objection for people'. Assertion, no conversion figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class. Free, one afternoon of PDP editing, no traffic or attribution required — exactly the CRO stage RSC is gated at. Distinct from what conversion-friction-audit currently holds: that skill covers returns/cancellation visibility, but nothing covers stating dispatch speed and shipping cost at the decision point, and shipping cost is a real objection at a $50.46 AOV on the Shopify side. Not higher because Amazon displays shipping and returns itself, so the gain is confined to the ~$875/mo Shopify channel.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add the three standard ecommerce objections — return window, dispatch speed, shipping cost — stated in short form immediately beside the add-to-cart button.

tactics.claim: Check that stated terms are internally consistent — a price shown in pounds alongside a '$75 free shipping' threshold implies overseas fulfilment and silently creates a delivery-time objection the page never answers.
tactics.mechanism: Buyers infer from inconsistencies. A mismatched currency or unit signals the seller is somewhere else, which manufactures a new unanswered doubt about how long delivery will take, so an inconsistency costs more than the missing information itself.
tactics.evidence: Specific observation on the live example page (GBP price, USD shipping threshold, plus contradictory dispatch times in two places). No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class and free to check, but the specific failure mode is weaker here: RSC is US-based selling primarily domestically, so the currency mismatch largely doesn't arise. The transferable version is narrow — make sure the free-shipping threshold, handling time and return window say the same thing on the PDP, in the cart, in the policy pages and in the Amazon listing. A one-time consistency pass, not a recurring lever, and unmeasurable at ~54 orders/month.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add a one-time consistency pass: shipping threshold, handling time and return window must state identical terms across PDP, cart, policy pages and Amazon listing.

tactics.claim: Reviews that are all dated within the same short window read as manufactured and undermine the credibility they were meant to provide.
tactics.mechanism: Buyers scan review dates as an authenticity check; a cluster suggests bulk solicitation or fabrication, so the proof block inverts and becomes a trust cost instead of a trust gain.
tactics.evidence: Direct observation on the example page — 'they all look around the same dates, which is a bit of a concern' — asserted, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable persuasion principle, age irrelevant, free to act on, and genuinely relevant at low volume: with ~54 orders/month a burst of post-purchase review requests produces exactly the same-week cluster described, so the actionable form is to drip requests continuously rather than in campaigns, and to show dates. Held at 5 because it is a hygiene constraint on existing review solicitation rather than a revenue mechanism of its own.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Constrain review solicitation: drip requests continuously rather than in batches so displayed review dates don't cluster and read as manufactured.

tactics.claim: Put clear step-by-step application instructions on the product page before purchase, because 'how easy is this actually to use' is itself a buying objection.
tactics.mechanism: Anything with a perceived learning curve makes the buyer silently doubt they'll succeed with it; showing the exact steps pre-purchase removes that doubt at the point of decision rather than after the box arrives.
tactics.evidence: Live teardown pointing at the example page's clear instruction block as good practice. Assertion, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class and an unusually exact category match: natural deodorant has a real how-much/how-often/what-happens-in-week-two question, and oral care likewise. Zero cost, solo-executable on the PDP and as an Amazon A+ block, no traffic or attribution required. Distinct from marketing-post-purchase-onboarding, which owns the insert and post-purchase sequence — this is the pre-purchase instance where instructions function as objection handling. Not higher because it sits adjacent to the published-results-timeline tactic and must be reconciled with the information-fatigue rule (accordion, not stacked above the fold).

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit
targetSkill.description: Add pre-purchase usage instructions as objection handling: show the exact application steps and week-by-week expectations on the PDP and in A+ content, collapsed into an accordion.

tactics.claim: Demonstrate the result rather than describing it — show the extreme proof (people attacking the protected phone with a knife) instead of only claiming the product is good.
tactics.mechanism: A stated claim is discounted; a visible stress test lets the buyer verify the outcome themselves in one glance, which is proof rather than assertion.
tactics.evidence: Creator's own critique that 'the result could be clearer' despite an otherwise strong page, citing existing knife-test content the brand isn't using. Assertion.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class. Executable solo at near-zero cost with a phone camera: a stated wear test (hot day, gym session, 12-hour workday, end-of-day shirt shot) is the deodorant equivalent, and it belongs in Amazon secondary image slots — the larger ~$1,800/mo channel — as well as the PDP. Capped at 6 because marketing-product-image-stack already owns transformation before/after imagery, so the additive claim is narrow (demonstration under stress, not just after-state), and body-care claims need care to stay defensible.

tactics.claim: A single-concept brand should sell the concept on its homepage — mechanism explanation, benefit icons, enough scientific-looking detail to earn belief, then the product range — rather than treating the homepage purely as a funnel into category pages the way multi-product retailers do.
tactics.mechanism: If the homepage does no selling, visitors arrive at a category page unpersuaded that the category is worth buying at all; doing the belief-building work up front means the product page only has to close, not convince.
tactics.evidence: Comparative observation across the teardowns — the single-product brand sells the concept on the homepage, wide-range retailers just funnel — presented as the more effective approach. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, free, solo-executable. Partially applicable: RSC has 12 SKUs across four categories, so it is the multi-product case the creator contrasts against, but it does have one hero concept (switching to a natural deodorant that actually works) worth selling on the homepage instead of a bare collection grid. Held at 5 because the homepage sits on the ~$875/mo Shopify side, gets low traffic, and retention — not first-visit persuasion — is the binding constraint.
